processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Bada: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As with other Bada large-leaf raw pu-erh, long dark olive leaves with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with Bada raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typically thick, large olive-green leaves, as with other Yunnan large-leaf tea.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about Manmai on its own. Bada tea generally is strong and bitter with a lasting sweetness and plum and honey aromas.

brewing.notes: As with other Bada teas, go light and short at first, since the bitterness builds fast.

vintage_note: Like other raw pu-erh, it is sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored. It is a small village name, and most Bada leaf goes out under the mountain's name, so ask which Manmai is meant.
description:
Manmai is a terroir name on Bada Mountain in Xiding township, Menghai County, listed alongside its better-known neighbour Zhanglang. Bada runs from about 1,580 to 2,000 metres and has old tea trees in Manmai among other villages.

The name is not unique. A Manmai Laozhai also appears among the Hekai villages near Menghun, and a Manmai village appears under Gasa in Jinghong, so a label saying only Manmai leaves real doubt about the place.

Processing would follow the usual raw pu-erh route. Little is recorded about how Manmai differs in the cup from the rest of Bada, where the general picture is strong bitterness, a lasting sweet return, and plum and honey.

Ask the seller for the mountain as well as the village, and for the year. Old-tree claims are common on Menghai teas and are hard for a buyer to check.
history: Little is documented about the history of tea at Manmai beyond its listing as a Bada terroir.
